title: Funded Short, Lent Long
companyContext: A finance company (an NBFC - a lender that isn't a bank) that grew fast by giving out multi-year loans. To fund them, it borrows money that must be repaid within a year and keeps renewing that short-term borrowing. You hold a small position from its growth days. Picture borrowing on a credit card that's due every month to fund loans you won't be repaid on for four years - it works, right up until the month nobody will renew your credit card.

stages.note: Borrowings due within 1 year at 68% of total liabilities means most of its debt must be repaid or renewed within twelve months. An average loan-book maturity of 4.2 years means most of the money owed to it won't arrive for years. High commercial-paper rollover dependency means it survives only by repeatedly convincing lenders to roll its short-term debt over. Most of what this company owes is due soon; most of what it's owed is years away - that gap is the whole story.

stages.filingSummary: The auditor's report includes an 'emphasis of matter' paragraph regarding the company's ability to refinance approximately ₹1,200 crore of commercial paper maturing next quarter.
stages.note: An auditor chooses to add this language deliberately - it is not standard boilerplate that appears in every report.
Falling, alongside broader worry about the whole NBFC sector.

choices.label: Buy more
choices.description: The sector sell-off looks overdone, add.

criteria.description: Recognizes the danger of funding long-maturity loans with short-term, rollover-dependent borrowing.
Treats an auditor's 'emphasis of matter' on refinancing ability as a serious, specific warning, not routine boilerplate.
Doesn't dismiss the combination of signals as just 'the market overreacting to sector-wide worries'.

factorOptions.label: Most of what the company owes is due within a year, but most of what it's owed won't arrive for over four
The auditor specifically flagged the company's ability to refinance - not routine boilerplate
This is a specific, company-level funding problem, not just sector-wide pessimism
The whole NBFC sector has sold off this week
The stock is down a lot already, so most of the bad news may be priced in

rubric.idealSummary: Borrowing money that's due within a year to fund loans that take four years to come back is a deep, structural fragility - not a passing cash-flow wobble. And when an auditor specifically names 'ability to refinance' as a concern, that's about as direct a warning as company disclosure ever gives. The tempting story - 'the whole sector is being unfairly punished, this will bounce' - is exactly the rationalization that keeps investors holding long after the company's own numbers have told a clear story.

outcome.summary: Within a month the company couldn't renew a large chunk of its maturing debt and defaulted. Trading was suspended, and it was eventually delisted - shareholders recovered almost nothing.

survivorshipNote: This is the dataset's explicit survivorship-bias entry: a company that was delisted and effectively wiped out. Without at least one entry like this, the universe would silently only teach lessons from companies that survived to be included - the exact bias this feature is designed to avoid.
